items.desc: New MBARI research has revealed that the sea cucumber Pelagothuria natatrix plays an important and unexpected role in the ocean's carbon cycle. items.desc: Quantum computers, computer systems that leverage the laws of quantum mechanics, store and process information using qubits (i.e., quantum bits). In many quantum computers, qubits are linked via entanglement, a quantum mechanical effect that connects particles in such a way that their shared state cannot be described as separate, independent states.

items.title: Is this the 'mathocalypse'? Why OpenAI's latest results dump has left mathematicians in shock
items.desc: Earlier this week, OpenAI published a trove of hundreds of mathematical results it claimed could "push the frontier of human knowledge." items.desc: The Center for the Creator Economy at Syracuse University—the nation's first academic center dedicated to the advancement of interdisciplinary academics, independent research, policy engagement and support for creator-based ventures—today released the findings from its inaugural industry Flash Report. Published monthly, these reports examine the issues creators, brands and audiences are talking about right now.

items.title: How much noise should we put up with? London and Copenhagen have different answers
items.desc: Traffic, trains, nightlife—in cities everywhere, there is a near-constant background hum that most people simply get used to.

items.title: Are autistic suspects likely to be disadvantaged in forensic interviews?
items.desc: A new study led by Flinders University finds both autistic and nonautistic suspects may be judged more harshly if any idiosyncratic behaviors in interviews stray beyond what observers consider normal. The research also undermines the widely held perspective—referred to as the "double empathy hypothesis"—that autistic people can better "read" differing intentions and motivations in other autistic people than nonautistic people can.

items.title: Walking through flames: Orangutans rescued in Indonesia fires
items.desc: The orangutan clings to the top of a mostly leafless tree in Indonesia's portion of Borneo as waves of thick smoke from the forest fires burning below waft over her.

items.title: Seals and sea lions get their hearing tested at Australia Zoo
items.desc: Scientists in Australia trained sea lions and seals to respond to a hearing test for research into how the marine mammals are affected by human-made noise.

items.title: Malaysia closes schools in capital, parts of country due to haze
items.desc: Malaysia closed schools in Kuala Lumpur and other parts of the country Friday as haze from fires in neighboring Indonesia again pushed local air quality to some of the world's worst levels.

items.title: Fish may look fine in urban waters but their genes tell a different story
items.desc: Blue damselfish, with their striking blue hue, are easy to spot, even along Okinawa's heavily urbanized coastlines. But while abundant, their gene activity reveals a hidden cost to living in human-impacted environments.

items.title: 'Molecular movie' finally reveals how penicillin is made
items.desc: Researchers from the University of Oxford and international collaborators have revealed previously unseen rapid chemical stages in the formation of β-lactam antibiotics like penicillin, offering insights that can support future antibiotic development. The findings have been published in Nature Catalysis.

items.title: 3D genome 'entanglement' may explain how cephalopods evolved complex brains
items.desc: Octopuses, squid and cuttlefish, collectively known as coleoid cephalopods, have evolved exceptionally large and elaborately structured nervous systems capable of complex behaviors such as problem-solving and rapid camouflage. A new study by scientists at the University of Vienna suggests that the origins of this complexity may lie not just in the genes themselves, but in how the genome is organized in 3D.

items.title: Hurricane Isaias strengthens en route to US Gulf Coast
items.desc: Isaias strengthened to a Category 2 hurricane on Thursday as it headed toward the U.S. Gulf Coast, the U.S. National Hurricane Center said, prompting mandatory evacuations and disrupting oil and gas production.

items.title: Four astronauts return to Earth after eight months in space
items.desc: Four astronauts returned to Earth from the International Space Station on Thursday after hurrying there eight months ago to replace an ailing colleague and his crew.

items.title: NASA astronauts splash down after 100 million miles in space
items.desc: NASA’s SpaceX Crew-12 astronauts have returned to Earth after 237 days in space, traveling more than 100 million miles and completing over 3,792 orbits while conducting research to prepare for future missions to the Moon and Mars. The mission also made history with record-setting spacewalk achievements and experiments that could transform medicine both in space and on Earth.

items.title: October’s night sky is full of cosmic tricks and treats
items.desc: October’s skies are packed with celestial surprises, from Jupiter disappearing behind the Moon to two meteor showers lighting up the darkness. NASA highlights four must-see events, including shooting stars from Halley’s Comet and a glowing Hunter’s Moon just before Halloween.

items.title: NASA is searching for hidden caves to build its first Moon base
items.desc: NASA is preparing for humanity’s first Moon base with three investigations that will hunt for underground shelters, uncover hidden ice, and track dangerous conditions on the lunar surface. The findings could reveal how astronauts can survive and thrive on the Moon while laying the groundwork for future journeys to Mars.

items.title: Scientists accidentally discover a genetic code that breaks the rules of life
items.desc: Scientists accidentally discovered a microscopic organism with a genetic code that breaks a rule researchers thought was nearly universal. While testing a new DNA sequencing technique, they examined a previously unknown protist collected from a freshwater pond at Oxford University. To their surprise, the organism uses two genetic signals that normally mark the end of a gene to encode two entirely different amino acids instead. These signals were previously thought to evolve together, making the discovery particularly remarkable.

items.title: Scientists find hidden materials that could improve batteries and solar fuels
items.desc: Scientists have uncovered a hidden world of “in-between” materials that briefly form as chemical ingredients are heated, revealing structures that conventional methods can miss. Among the discoveries is a previously unknown form of bismuth vanadate, a material widely studied for using sunlight to help produce clean hydrogen. The new version has a different atomic structure and interacts with light in a strikingly different way, potentially opening new possibilities for solar fuels, catalysts, and electronics.

items.title: This “golden tree” coral was too strange for any known family
items.desc: A brilliant yellow coral discovered off Costa Rica proved so unusual that scientists had to create an entirely new family to classify it. The meter-tall colonies rise from seafloors covered in brittle stars, inspiring the Tolkien-inspired name Laurinque elenya, or “golden tree of the stars.” Advanced genetic analysis revealed that the coral belongs to a previously unknown evolutionary lineage.

items.title: Scientists found Homo erectus 200,000 years earlier than expected
items.desc: New fossils from South Africa are reshaping the story of early human evolution. Researchers have described 18 hominin fossils from Drimolen Cave, including an adult Homo erectus skull fragment dated to about 2 million years ago, supporting evidence that the species appeared in southern Africa roughly 200,000 years earlier than long thought. The finds also reveal that Paranthropus robustus, which lived alongside Homo erectus, was gradually evolving even larger teeth and stronger chewing muscles as the climate changed.

items.title: NASA’s Webb finds signs of Mars-sized worlds smashing together
items.desc: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope is giving astronomers a glimpse of the kinds of violent collisions that may have shaped our own solar system, including the giant impact thought to have created the Moon. By studying 21 rare “extreme debris disks” around young stars, researchers found that their dust can reveal the scale and intensity of planetary collisions.

items.title: A 9-billion-year-old signal could help explain dark energy
items.desc: A Canadian radio telescope has detected the faint glow of hydrogen from billions of years ago using only its own observations, proving a long-awaited way to map the distant universe can actually work. CHIME can use this hydrogen signal to trace how matter is spread across space and measure how the universe has expanded over time, offering a powerful new way to investigate dark energy.

items.title: Bacteria turn a virus’ own weapon against it
items.desc: Researchers have uncovered a new way bacteria detect viral attacks: a virus-produced enzyme cuts a bacterial sensor protein, triggering a self-destructing immune response. The discovery could lead to more effective phage therapies against antibiotic-resistant bacteria and provide insight into ancient immune mechanisms shared with humans.

items.title: FDA-approved epilepsy drug may help reverse osteoarthritis damage
items.desc: Researchers at Yale have identified a promising new approach to osteoarthritis that could do more than simply ease pain. The epilepsy drug lacosamide appears to block a protein involved in both pain signaling and cartilage destruction, helping damaged joints shift back toward repair in preclinical studies.

items.title: A quantum prediction from 1931 just came to life
items.desc: Nearly a century after physicist Hans Bethe predicted them, scientists have created and directly observed unusual quantum states known as “Bethe strings” in an ultracold gas. By cooling cesium atoms to near absolute zero and trapping them in thousands of tiny one-dimensional tubes, researchers were able to make groups of atoms bind together without ordinary chemical bonds. These strange clusters could contain six or more particles and even collide with one another without falling apart.

items.title: Einstein Probe reveals a hidden phase of neutron star collisions
items.desc: Einstein Probe revealed nearly 10 minutes of soft X-ray activity following a short gamma-ray burst, exposing a phase of neutron star mergers that previous missions may have missed. The prolonged emission could have been powered by a newly formed magnetar and may provide a valuable new counterpart to gravitational-wave signals.

items.title: Just 7 days of strength training started shrinking fat cells in mice
items.desc: Just seven strength-training sessions helped obese mice shrink visceral fat cells and reactivate molecular pathways involved in burning stored fat, despite no change in overall body weight. The findings suggest some benefits of resistance exercise may begin long before weight loss becomes visible, though the results still need to be confirmed in humans.

items.title: Scientists changed how zoo lions eat. Their wild side came out
items.desc: Giving zoo lions whole carcasses on a feast-and-fast schedule appears to bring out more natural behavior. The lions spent nearly three times longer feeding, engaged in more tearing and manipulating of food, and rested more heavily after meals. Their activity then increased gradually during the fasting period, closely resembling the rhythm seen in wild lions.

items.title: Fukuyama, Thiel, and the Revenge of the Last Man
items.desc: In his new memoir, Francis Fukuyama attempts to redeem his thesis about the end of history. But Peter Thiel’s ongoing quest to escape government oversight and wrest control of the future from democratic majorities makes a mockery of his argument all over again.

items.title: The Journalists’ Revolt Against AI Scraping
items.desc: Big Tech’s oligopolistic dominance has prevented the news industry from developing a sustainable business model for the digital age—a crisis that AI is exacerbating. To preserve this important pillar of democracy, the Spanish-language publisher Editorial Perfil is suing OpenAI and Microsoft for copyright infringement.

items.title: MAGA’s Self-Destructive Culture War
items.desc: Polls suggest that MAGA fanaticism might not be playing so well outside US President Donald Trump’s loyal base. But if the Democrats want to retake one or both chambers of Congress, they should concentrate on the economy and not answer Republican extremism with a culture war of their own.

items.title: How to Break the German Malaise
items.desc: For too long, Germany’s political and corporate elite coasted on the country’s postwar economic and political success story, avoiding difficult but necessary reforms that could have kept extremist populist parties at bay. Now that the barbarians are at the gates, mainstream elites must rethink everything.

items.title: Europe’s Place in the Global Redivision of Labor
items.desc: While the US continues to lead in software, some high-tech sectors, and hydrocarbons, China is becoming increasingly competitive in many high-tech, capital-intensive sectors, not least those once dominated by Europe. The EU does have a relative advantage in this new economic order, if only its leaders would recognize it.

items.title: The World Has Passed Peak Trump
items.desc: US President Donald Trump, previously the most powerful, unpredictable force on the international stage, has now passed the peak of his ability to disrupt the international order. With his approval ratings collapsing, foreign leaders whose tenures will extend beyond his own are starting to write him off.

items.title: Global Financial Reform that Centers African Women
items.desc: While gender-equality objectives often fall by the wayside in times of upheaval, the current rupture in the multilateral order creates an opportunity to build a debt architecture that will deliver for the women of Africa. The first steps toward this goal can be taken at this month’s IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok.

items.title: How Africa Can Leverage the US-China Thaw
items.desc: As dollar borrowing costs soar, Chinese rates are approaching record lows. This divergence, combined with the US-China thaw, creates an opportunity for African governments: partner with the US on gas and with China on solar and storage, and tap lower-cost Asian capital markets to finance investments in both.

items.title: Closing NATO’s Deterrence Gap
items.desc: With Russian provocations against NATO member states growing more frequent, the alliance urgently needs to develop a credible doctrine of punitive deterrence to guide its response to acts of aggression that fall below the threshold of war. Mere territorial defense is not enough.

items.title: The India-Pakistan Cold War
items.desc: The current stalemate between India and Pakistan should be viewed not as a pause between rounds of negotiation, but rather as part of a deliberate Indian strategy of disengagement. India will return to the negotiating table only after Pakistan dismantles, comprehensively and verifiably, its state-supported terrorist networks.

items.title: The Next Era of Reform Must Be About Capability
items.desc: Economic development should no longer be measured solely by how much finance is mobilized or how much fiscal space is created. It must also be judged by whether countries emerge more capable of setting their own priorities, responding to challenges, and seizing new opportunities to shape their own future.

items.title: With AI, Sharing Is Caring
items.desc: Although the public's distrust of Big Tech is understandable, given past experience, that is not a reason to starve AI models of the information and data they will need to be useful. If serving the public interest is the goal, everyone relying on the technology's output has a duty to provide high-quality input.

items.title: Why the US-China Trade Truce Matters
items.desc: Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump’s agreement to extend their trade truce reflects the fact that both sides have leverage over the other. In a world where the rules-based trading system is not functioning, the current fragile equilibrium may be the best one can hope for.

items.title: Brazil’s Voters Have Moved
items.desc: A strong performance by the right-wing, Donald Trump-aligned candidate in the first round of Brazil’s presidential election demonstrates that the left-wing ruling party has failed to keep up with the times. The Brazilian electorate is older, more devout, and more preoccupied with crime and personal security than it once was.

items.title: Does Inclusive Finance Really Need Stablecoins?
items.desc: Today, 1.3 billion adults—more than half of them women—remain excluded from the formal financial system, and lower-income consumers still struggle to find and access the financial products and services they need.
